Triggers.value: A specific texture associated with the event

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't deal with even the slightest upset
Nothing good can happen to me anymore
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: The trigger items are not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of police violence. Snake-related cues and fire/flames do not plausibly connect to police violence unless there were unusual event details, and no other selected items suggest such a context. This makes the trigger profile hard to explain for the same trauma.

Within Memory, 'Vivid Memory' and 'Memory Gaps' can coexist in PTSD, but 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with a severe PTSD presentation and with the memory disturbance pattern implied by the other memory items. It suggests unusually easy narrative access despite simultaneously endorsing vivid re-experiencing and amnestic gaps, which is internally inconsistent here.

Fire/flames is hard to reconcile as a trauma trigger for police violence in the absence of any corroborating memory or appraisal content linking the trauma to fire; 'Police' as an authority trigger fits, but 'fire/flames' appears trauma-incongruent for this profile.

issues.item: Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
issues.explanation: The Memory node contains a direct internal contradiction: endorsing very clear/detailed memories, irretrievable gaps, and very easy verbal access all together is not clinically coherent as stated. Vivid memory can coexist with some gaps, but pairing both with 'I can talk about what happened very easily' strongly conflicts with a severe PTSD profile and with the fragmented/distressing memory pattern implied by the other memory items.

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with marked trauma-memory disruption indicated by both severe memory gaps and fragmented, disconnected recollections. Those memory items imply impaired coherent access to the trauma narrative, making very easy verbal access hard to reconcile clinically in the same profile.

vignette: Priya Desai still remembers the exact moment the evening air turned to ice. She had been walking past the community center after returning a borrowed book, her hands wrapped around a paper bag of oranges, when a marked sedan pulled alongside the curb. Two officers stepped out, their dark uniforms stark against the streetlights, and barked a sudden, commanding request for identification. When Priya hesitated, one officer lunged forward, his gloved hand clamping onto her wrist. The coarse, stiff weave of the tactical fabric scraped against her skin, and the sheer authority in his voice triggered a panic she could not suppress. As they pressed her against the damp pavement, the rough grit of the sidewalk against her cheek and the heavy, synchronized tread of their boots became inescapable anchors in a scene she could never piece together. Years later, at seventy-three, she understands precisely why those specific sensations hold such terror: the sudden command of a uniformed figure, the unmistakable presence of authority, and that same unyielding fabric against her skin instantly transport her back to the moment her body was overpowered by men who held all the power. In the weeks that followed, the fragmented pieces of the arrest would surface without warning, usually when she was sorting through client samples in her design studio. A discarded piece of burlap or a heavy wool blanket from a warehouse shipment would suddenly pull a half-remembered image to the surface—the same rough texture that had pressed against her during the seizure. These disjointed memories did not arrive with context; they simply flooded her senses, turning a quiet Tuesday in her showroom into a moment of paralyzing recall. The fragmented pieces would surface without warning, usually when she was sorting through client samples. A discarded piece of burlap or a heavy wool blanket from a warehouse shipment would suddenly pull a half-remembered image to the surface—the same rough texture that had pressed against her during the seizure. These disjointed memories did not arrive with context; they simply flooded her senses, turning a quiet Tuesday in her showroom into a moment of paralyzing recall. This fragmented recall soon warped her understanding of her own resilience. Because she was certain she could not cope with even the slightest upset, her mind began to protect itself by refusing to cooperate. The gaps in her recollection widened into aching voids, and the fragments she could access refused to cohere into a narrative. She would sit at her drafting table, tracing the same blueprints for hours, trying to pin down what had happened, but the words would catch in her throat. She knew what had occurred, yet the inability to find language for the trauma made the blanks feel even wider. This quiet resignation and the growing certainty that she would never recover tightened her chest, making every minor demand at work feel insurmountable. Her shifting beliefs about her own vulnerability kept her nervous system locked in a state of high alert. This conviction that her body was a traitor, constantly sounding alarms as if she were still pinned to the pavement, meant she could no longer tolerate ordinary stimuli. When a new security guard in a crisp navy uniform walked into her studio to discuss a contract, the visual of the uniform immediately made her heart hammer. The mere presence of authority figures became unbearable, not because of any recent threat, but because her own physiological alarms had dialed their sensitivity so high that a uniformed presence felt like a direct escalation. The more she braced for threat, the more her body reacted to ordinary stimuli, which in turn made the original triggers feel even more overwhelming. Every time the studio doorway opened, the cycle tightened further. When the coarse burlap from a client’s upholstery sample brushed her forearm, the tactile sensation made her feel utterly incapable of handling the moment. Her body kept reacting as if she were still in danger, and this physical alarm convinced her that nothing good could happen anymore. The trigger did not simply startle her; it confirmed her fear that she was too fragile to navigate a world that demanded constant vigilance. Over the months, this pattern eroded her professional life. She stopped hosting clients in her studio, preferring video calls to avoid the physical space where textures and authority figures might intrude. Her reputation for meticulous, tactile design work faded, replaced by unexplained cancellations and abrupt withdrawals. Now, Priya sits on her sofa, surrounded by the quiet of her widow’s home. Her husband had passed years ago, and while grief was its own heavy companion, it was the police encounter that left her life stripped of color. She finally sought help after a recent trip to a hospital for a minor appointment, where a uniformed staff member handed her a clipboard. The moment she felt the rough, cheap paper and heard the clipped instructions, her hands shook uncontrollably, and she was certain she would collapse again. She is hoping, more than anything, to find a way to quiet the physical alarms and reclaim the spaces she once loved. What frightens her most is that her own body and mind will never stop sounding the siren, leaving her trapped in a past she cannot quite remember but cannot escape.
